title: Domain Coverage: From Three Model Families to the Book's Chapters
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-13 from the published page (posts/domain-coverage/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the page, in its order; tables are recorded as evidence of the paragraph they follow. Intent, acceptance criteria and role are copied unchanged from journal-spec.json; the journal spec gives a reference page no thesis, so the thesis here is the page's own and only orders its sections. A light pass for a lookup page: the entries were checked for consistency, not rewritten.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader finds the chapter that covers a capability, or learns that it is left out and why.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: where does the book cover reviews and ratings, where does batch and lot traceability stand, and is route planning for an own delivery fleet in the book?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Reviews, ratings and Q&A are covered in commerce-search-and-discovery as discovery and trust data, with the fake-review rule in commerce-regulation. Lot traceability is thin: product-safety information in commerce-regulation, lots and recalls not modeled in any chapter; food, cosmetics and pharma readers should treat the lot as a dimension of the stock ledger. Route planning for an own fleet is left out: a logistics subject with its own software, and Kestrel & Pine ships with carriers.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader says what the planning models are, why they are not evidence, and what the book adds that they lack.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: what are the models behind the book's planning, may a claim about Shopify's internal systems be sourced to them, and name two things the book covers that the models do not?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Productscape domain models the author maintains, inferred from public product behavior (a hosted platform of the Shopify kind, a marketplace of the Amazon kind, nine specialist products), with a modeled seed value for every number; they are planning maps, not evidence of any company's internal systems, so no. The models have no integration layer (the book's Part VI), no scale-stage view, no failure patterns, no journey across products (Part IX) and nothing about choosing, changing or organizing (Part X).

acceptance_criteria.expected: Tables showing which chapter covers each business job and which topics are outside the book's scope, and how that coverage differs from the eleven Productscape models used in planning (a merchant platform, a retail marketplace, nine specialist products); for the argument itself, commerce-capability-map and boundaries-and-systems-of-record. Material: the models and the written chapters, with the models stated not to be evidence about companies.

thesis.question: Which research models stand behind the book, and which chapters cover them?
thesis.claim: Eleven Productscape models in three families, inferred from public product behavior, stand behind the book's plan; each of their capabilities is sent to the chapter that covers it, or named as thin or left out with a reason, and the book adds the joins the models lack, so the models serve as a planning map and never as evidence about a company.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a coverage page only records the author's planning: a reader searches the chapters for a topic, and a model drawn from a real product's behavior is good enough evidence of how that product is built.
thesis.so_what: A reader finds the chapter for the system they own by the job it does, checks the left-out list against their business before relying on the book as a complete map, and never cites a model for a fact about Shopify, Amazon or a specialist vendor.
thesis.how_why: The digest lists 152 distinct capabilities across the models; the rows were placed from the chapter contracts and checked by text search against the written chapters, which moved three gaps into chapters and found six more thin spots. The models were drawn one product at a time, so they have no integration layer, scale stages, failure patterns or cross-product journeys; the book's Parts VI, IX and X and its failure patterns supply them.

supporting_claims.claim: The models are capability inventories inferred from public product behavior with seed values, so they are planning maps and never a source for a fact about a company.
Every capability of the models is sent to a primary chapter, read either by capability, grouped by the book's parts, or by model.
The capabilities the book covers thinly or leaves out are named, each with the reason.
The book departs from the models' product-by-product shape and adds the joins between products.
The models' personas map to the book's reader roles, a Kestrel & Pine seat and starting chapters, so the page doubles as a reading route.

role.contribution: Opens the reference part and sends a reader from a capability to its chapter, saying plainly what is left out and that the planning models are not evidence.

flow.rationale: What the models are comes first, because every table that follows is read under the rule that they are maps, not evidence. The full map by capability and then by model follows; the gaps, the departures and the personas each narrow it to one question a reader brings (is my job left out, why does the book not copy the models, where do I start). Putting the gaps before the map would list exceptions to a map the reader has not seen.

hook.content: Commerce spans more business jobs than one book can cover equally: these pages show where each one is covered, what is left out, and where the records, terms and sources live.

bridge.from_reader_world: The reader has met cards, terms and sources in the chapters, each introduced where it was needed, and arrives with a business job or system to look up.
bridge.to_topic: The reference pages gather that material for lookup, and this one sends a job to its chapter and says what the book leaves out.
